messages.body_plain:
Hi,
You can run uere.fit() on individual deployments or on a list of multiple deployments (under the assumption of everything being equal) and compare. There is an example in vignette('error').
I don't see that the file is exactly in Movebank format, as you don't have a timestamp column, but separate date and time columns... not that this would hurt the calibration step too much, but it would mess up tracking data analysis.
I don't see any error information columns in your data. You don't have any DOP values or anything else? Is there some more complete dataset that these came from?
I don't recommend editing your data in Excel, as it has a tendency to mangle timestamp formats.
Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Summarizing large AKDE overlap results
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for making such an excellent spatial analytical tool available to general users. Really great method!

Three quick questions:

1. I have a large old-school radiotelemetry dataset of multiple individual birds tracked across multiple years. I am breaking my ctmm analyses into different time windows to explore different behavioral events (mostly seasonal). As a result, I have large amounts of BC and AKDE range overlap output values across many individual pairs and time windows. What would you recommend as a good method for summarizing these many overlap values? Should I simply report the individual birds that had the highest/lowest overlap values within each time window? Or is there a statistically appropriate method to summarize and present these results? I am trying to avoid large tables!

2. The bird telemetry dataset I am analyzing was collected by simply relocating each individual bird in the field via VHF once per day, so autocorrelation is low. However, this does also mean that trajectory speed/distance values are not informative. The birds  mostly occupied highly overlapping home ranges within a relatively small area of habitat - I assume that I should still report only on range overlap across the 95% AKDE boundaries and not the inner 50% core boundaries (due to the estimation of the CI values)? I am trying to detect incidences where birds did not spatiotemporally interact, which is proving difficult due to the coarse location data sampling rate and their highly overlapping ranges.

3. Given the coarse sampling rate of my location data and the high range overlap values I derived, would the CDE framework be useful to further explore interactions between these birds? Or is CDE better for studying high sampling rate GPS data acquired from species with ranges that are conterminous with lower levels of overlap (e.g. abutting territories)?

I am happy to share some example data and results if that would help.

Regards & thanks,
  James

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I hope you're having a good start to the year.

This one's more of a general question on transferring location error information estimated in ctmm package into other anlayses, so not strictly a ctmm query, but hoping you might be able to point me in the right direction!

I'm currently revisiting some old analyses to see if I can update them to be error-informed, including some behavioral partitioning using smoove. At this stage, it's largely academic as the magnitude of location error from the GPS collars we have is really very small relative to the scale of movement at current data resolution, but figured it's a good thing to have worked out for use in the future as we're getting in increasingly higher resolution fixes as battery life improves...

Thanks to the pointers in the smoove vignette and your error paper, I can see that I need to do this by passing arguments to crwMLE,  presumably at the estimate UCVM stage.  So far, I haven't really interacted much with the crawl package -- so still working out exactly what I need to feed into this/how it works.

>From what I can gather, the crwMLE function relies on ellipse error params provided by Argos devices, so I need to fill these in somehow for GPS data based on the error radius of locations. I've never worked wth Argos data, but it seems like the info I am looking for relates to major/minor axis error (length in metres) and orientation. What I am struggling with at the moment, is how I can use the location error information from the ctmm calibration process to do this. Given the error ellipses you can plot from calibrated data in ctmm look circular, I am assuming that there will be the same values for x/y error -- and it seems likely that I can somehow get the info I need from the VAR.xy column.

I've looked a bit through the crawl and also the momentuHMM literature given it also leverages the crwMLE function, and found an example in the momentuHMM vignette where they assume "a 50 m isotropic error ellipse" for the measurement error model part (for track prediction) -- they include this by using the function crawl::argosDiag2Cov (which takes major/minor axis info, and angle orientation of major axis from North for each observation; 50, 50, 0 in this case) to give: log standard deviation of the location error in x coord, same for y -- plus correlation of the location error ellipse, in this case 0. They then pass the output to the error model arguments in the crawLME function to be used as the location error models for long/lat. (in form of ~ log sd location error - 1).

Here they pass a single set of values, which I'm assuming corresponds to assuming homoskedastic error model, but could equally be a vector of values -- if what I'm aiming for is the log standard deviation of location error -- and the VAR.xy column is the variance of location error (?) -- then would log of sqrt of VAR.xy give me what I am looking for? I will admit, I am not 100% sure why use the log of the standard deviation of location error, other than this seems to be what crawl is asking for. The only other thing I thought might be another option is to use RMS UERE estimate * DOP for each observation to generate a value for location error, but not really sure how this would then translate to "length" of each axis. Alternatively, if I am barking up the totally wrong tree, that would also be of use to know!!

Thanks,

Gen

messages.subject: Re: Summarizing large AKDE overlap results
messages.body_plain:
Thanks James,
As far as producing a summary statistic or summary comparison, I haven't worked out an ideal way to do this. There are two complications--- (1) the uncertainties are often large and (2) the estimates are calculated pairwise and are very correlated. As far as just relaying the descriptive statistics, I would produce a plot similar to what ctmmweb does ( https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.05.11.087932v1.full has an example ). If you want, I can implement that style of plot in ctmm, but ctmmweb functions can also be called from R.
The overlap calculated in ctmm is a statistical overlap of the two distributions, which is really more of a similarity measure and not a geometric overlap, though it has a straightforward geometric interpretation when space use is uniform. With the statistical approach here, the advantages are that there is no ad hoc choice of % coverage and space use is not assumed to be uniform.
As with home-range estimation, sampling rate isn't really the most relevant factor, as it gives you diminishing returns on the estimate quality. The CDE could still be useful for looking at where potential interactions take place. The quality of the estimate should be conveyed by the size of the corresponding uncertainty.
As for more direct measures of potential interaction, relative encounter rates are calculated as a side effect when calculating the CDE, but their uncertainties aren't quantified and so they aren't yet exposed to the end user yet. That would be a good paper if I had someone willing to lead it, but I'm kind of strapped at the moment.

Best,
Chris

Hi Gen,

You appear to be on the right track. VAR.xy=VAR[x]=VAR[y] is the circular variance and log(sqrt(VAR.xy)) would be the log of the standard deviation. RMS[UERE] * DOP is proportional to the standard deviation that you want, but there is a sqrt(2) in the definition, because the x and y variances are summed with HDOP.

Best,
Chris

Hi Adrian,

I fixed a bug and added the ability to predict/simulate both horizontally and vertically, so that complete=TRUE can be performed. You can update the package via devtools::install_github("ctmm-initiative/ctmm")
Below is the sample code I ran and the output. The vertical errors were improved by predict(), but they are still pretty large.

##read data for one day of Anonymous (ASY - BLVU)

DATA <- as.telemetry("../DATA/Adrian Naveda-Rodríguez/v1.csv")

##read calibration data
CALI <- as.telemetry("../DATA/Adrian Naveda-Rodríguez/Calibration data CTT E-400 MB unit 12340 Nov15-21.csv")
#calibrate
UERE <- uere.fit(CALI) # only using calibration data
uere(DATA) <- UERE

# fit vertical movement model
zSVF <- variogram(DATA, axes="z")
GUESS <- ctmm.guess(DATA,variogram=zSVF,CTMM=ctmm(error=TRUE),interactive=F)
zFIT <- ctmm.select(DATA,GUESS,trace=2)
zoom(zSVF,CTMM=zFIT)

# fit horizontal movement model
SVF <- variogram(DATA)
GUESS <- ctmm.guess(DATA,CTMM=ctmm(error=TRUE),interactive=F)
FIT <- ctmm.select(DATA,GUESS,trace=2)
zoom(SVF,CTMM=FIT)

# predict locations
PRED <- predict(DATA,CTMM=FIT,VMM=zFIT,complete=TRUE)

# color by time
COL <- color(PRED,by="time")

par(mfrow=c(2,1))
plot(PRED,col=COL,velocity=TRUE)
CI.lo <- PRED$z-1.96*sqrt(PRED$COV.z.z)
CI.hi <- PRED$z+1.96*sqrt(PRED$COV.z.z)
plot(PRED$timestamp,PRED$z,pch=16,col=COL,xlab="Time",ylab="Altitude (m)",ylim=range(CI.lo,CI.hi))
arrows(PRED$timestamp,CI.lo,PRED$timestamp,CI.hi,angle=90,length=0.05,code=3,col=COL)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))

messages.subject: Re: GPS Unit calibration
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

1. You can input calibration data from multiple GPS devices that are of the same type, in a list, to uere.fit(). The output model assumes they are all behaving similarly, which is usually but not always the case. You can then check the goodness of fit of the joint model versus the individualized models. There is a simple example in vignette('error').
3. GPS errors tend to be heteroskedastic and while uere.fit() estimates some parameters, others (HDOP) must be supplied by the device as they vary by fix. I would try importing the EHPE column as an HDOP column if it is supposed to represent expected horizontal error. I looked at your attached calibration data and a homoskedastic error model slightly outperformed EHPE informed error, but the reception was generally very good and the results were very similar. EHPE might look better in other cases where the signal quality is poorer and the assumption of homoskedasticity is not as good. Also, the sampling here seems to be 1Hz (I assume this is one device?) whereas GPS location estimates tend to be autocorrelated over a 1-2 minute timescale, so as a warning this will overestimate AIC differences and underestimate CI widths.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gen,

The proper way to analyze this kind of data is with a model like this: https://movementecologyjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s40462-020-00199-6
The observation model is very different than GPS/Argos/VHF currently supported by ctmm. I'd like to get support into ctmm, but that will be a major effort (possibly in the next grant).

If you put this kind of data into location tracking methods, then the results become bad when the scales of movement are smaller than or comparable to the the grid resolution. So for coarse data, an (A)KDE home-range estimate might look okay if the bandwidth > grid scale, but with more data, you will start to see excess density at the stations.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gen,

I guess you could try fitting with location error equal to the detection radius, and then taking the maximum of the optimal bandwidth (under the wrong observation model) and the spatial resolution of the station grid. Then there are internal functions that you could use to create the density estimate given an arbitrary bandwidth (or another package like ks).

I've also been talking to someone with mark-capture-recapture data about taking the (A)KDE PDF evaluated at the stations, interpolating those point estimates over the whole domain, and then renormalizing the interpolated density to integrate to 1. That would at least give you something that is asymptotically consistent at the station locations and smoothly varying between.

Best,
Chris
